kurz: Why an option can lose value even when the direction of the price was predicted correctly, and which six variables determine its price.

bloecke.md: An option premium is made up of two components that arise in very different ways. The first can be read off exactly on any trading day and does not depend on anyone's opinion. The second is a price that the buyer pays for expectations. It determines whether an investor loses money despite a correct price forecast.

bloecke.formel:
Premium = intrinsic value + time value

intrinsic value (call) = max(S − K, 0)
intrinsic value (put)  = max(K − S, 0)
bloecke.erklaerung: The intrinsic value is the amount that immediate exercise would bring in. It can never be negative, because the holder is entitled but not obliged to exercise. If they do not exercise, they lose nothing further. The time value is the rest of the premium, that is, the extra paid for the fact that something can still happen before expiry.

bloecke.md:
The share is at €100, the remaining term is half a year, volatility is 25% and the interest rate 2.5%. All prices are rounded values from the standard model:

- A call with a strike price of €90 costs €13.62, of which €10.00 is intrinsic value and €3.62 time value.
- A call with a strike price of €110 costs €3.81. It has no intrinsic value; its price is entirely time value.
- A put with a strike price of €110 costs €12.45, of which €10.00 is intrinsic value and €2.45 time value.

If the share stays at €100 for half a year, the 110 call expires worthless. The buyer was not wrong about the direction; the price simply did not move. Nevertheless, they lose their entire outlay.

## Moneyness

[[Moneyness]] describes the position of the price relative to the strike price. A call is **in the money** (ITM) if S is above K, **at the money** (ATM) if S is roughly equal to K, and **out of the money** (OTM) if S is below K. For a put, it is the mirror image. Only options in the money have intrinsic value. Options out of the money consist of 100% time value, even if a price of €3.81 looks like a small outlay.

bloecke.titel: Breakdown of the premium, share at €100, remaining term of half a year
Components of a call by strike price
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation with a share price of €100, a term of half a year and 25% volatility. The intrinsic value rises linearly to the left; the time value is highest at the money.

bloecke.md: The time value is highest at the money, because there every small price movement determines whether or not the option will be worth something in the end. Uncertainty about the outcome is greatest there, and it is this uncertainty that the buyer pays for. Deep in the money, the option behaves almost like the underlying itself, and its time value falls to little more than the interest advantage over buying directly. Far out of the money, the option ends in the money so rarely that nobody pays much for it.

## How the time value declines

On the expiry date, the time value must be zero, otherwise there would be a riskless profit. Until then, however, it declines unevenly. It roughly follows the square root of the remaining term. Half of the time value is therefore only lost when just a quarter of the term remains.

bloecke.titel: Time value of a call over the remaining term
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation with a constant share price of €100, 25% volatility and a 2.5% interest rate. Time runs from right to left. At the money, the time value is greatest and falls most steeply towards the end.

bloecke.md:
The at-the-money call with a term of twelve months has €11.02 of time value.

- In the first 60 days, it loses €1.04, which is around 1.7 cents per day.
- In the last 30 days, it loses €2.96, which is around 10 cents per day.
- After three quarters of the term, with 90 days remaining, €5.25 is still left, that is, just under half.

At the end, the daily loss of value is about six times as high as at the start. Investors who expect a price movement within three months therefore do not necessarily have to buy the three-month option. A longer contract costs more but loses value much more slowly over those three months.

bloecke.erklaerung: The formula is used for mental arithmetic with at-the-money options and low interest rates. With S = €100, σ = 25%, T = 0.5 and an interest rate of zero, it gives €7.07 compared with a model price of €7.03, and €10.00 compared with €9.95 for one year. With the 2.5% interest rate from the other examples, the model price is €7.63. The formula also shows how the price is structured. The time value grows in proportion to volatility, but only with the square root of time. Four times the term therefore costs only twice the price.
variablen: expected volatility p.a. as a decimal

bloecke.md: Short-dated options far out of the money seem cheap because their price is low. However, they are very likely to lose 100% of their value, because their price consists solely of time value, and that has to fall to zero. The low price therefore says little about the risk. With options that you buy, the outlay is the maximum loss, and with these options it occurs in most cases.

## Six factors that determine the option price

Every option valuation uses six inputs: the price of the underlying, the strike price, the remaining term, volatility, the risk-free rate and the expected dividend. Five of them can be read off. Volatility is the only unknown and is the subject of a separate lesson. The following table shows the direction in which each variable acts. It is calculated for a call and a put with a strike price of €100 on a share at €100 with a term of half a year. The starting prices are €7.63 for the call and €6.39 for the put.

bloecke.titel: Effect of a single change on the premium
zeilen: Opposite directions; together, the amounts come to exactly €1.
For the call, the purchase price rises; for the put, the sale price.
Both lose time value, regardless of direction.
More fluctuation raises both prices by exactly the same amount.
The strike price is discounted more heavily.
Distributions lower the expected future price.

bloecke.titel: Direction and size of the six influences
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation of the change in the premium in euros compared with €7.63 (call) and €6.39 (put). Only remaining term and volatility move both prices in the same direction, volatility by the same amount.

bloecke.md:
Two rows of the table often surprise beginners. A rising interest rate increases the value of the call, because its buyer only has to pay the purchase price later and can earn interest on the money until then. For the put, it is the other way round, because the sale proceeds only come in later. A higher dividend lowers the value of the call, because the price falls by the amount of the distribution on the ex-dividend date and the option holder receives no dividend. The dividend therefore acts solely through the price.

The fact that volatility affects the call and the put by exactly the same amount follows from a relationship that requires no valuation model at all.

## Put-call parity

The derivation uses two packages, both with European options on the same underlying, with the same strike price K and the same expiry date.

Package A consists of a call and cash equal to K, discounted to today.
Package B consists of a put and a share.

On the expiry date, the cash in package A has grown to exactly K. If the price is above K, the call is exercised and the money is used to buy the share, leaving the value S. If it is below K, the call expires, leaving the amount K. Package A is therefore worth max(S, K). In package B, if the price is below K, the put is exercised and the share is sold for K. If the price is above K, the share remains in the package and is worth S. Package B is thus also worth max(S, K), at every possible price on the expiry date and not just on average. Two packages with identical payoffs must cost the same today. Otherwise, you could buy the cheaper one, sell the more expensive one and make a risk-free profit.

bloecke.formel:
C − P = S − K × e^(−r×T)

with dividend yield q:
C − P = S × e^(−q×T) − K × e^(−r×T)
bloecke.erklaerung: Parity holds for European options with the same strike price and expiry. It is based solely on arbitrage and presupposes nothing about volatility, distribution or investor behaviour. That is why it holds even if every valuation model is wrong.
bloecke.beispiel: Share €100, K = €100, T = 0.5 years, r = 2.5%: C − P = 100 − 98.76 = €1.24. The model prices of €7.63 and €6.39 satisfy the equation exactly.

bloecke.md:
With American options, which may be exercised at any time, the equation becomes an inequality, because the right to early exercise has additional value. In practice, moreover, the equation only holds within a band. Bid-ask spreads, order fees, different borrowing and lending rates and restrictions on short selling prevent small deviations from being exploited. Private investors who believe they have found a violation of parity have usually overlooked the fact that the two prices were quoted at different times or on different sides of the spread.

The relationship is nevertheless useful. It follows from it that a protective put (share plus put) has the same payoff as a call plus a bond. Every hedged share position can therefore also be represented as an option position, and vice versa. Parity also explains why volatility has the same effect on the call and the put. The right-hand side of the equation contains no volatility, so any change in σ must shift both prices by the same amount.

## Practice in Germany

On Eurex, index options are quoted in points. For the EURO STOXX 50, one index point corresponds to €10 per contract. A premium of 30 points therefore costs €300. Overlooking the multiplier is one of the most common beginner mistakes.

Investors without access to the derivatives exchange find the time value of warrants in the **warrant premium** (Aufgeld). It states by what percentage acquiring the underlying via the warrant is more expensive than buying it directly. For warrants in the money or at the money, it corresponds to the time value as a percentage of the price; for warrants out of the money, the distance between strike price and price is added.

bloecke.formel: Warrant premium (call) = (K + warrant price ÷ ratio − S) ÷ S
bloecke.erklaerung: Example: share €100, strike price €100, ratio 0.1, warrant price €1.00. Calculated for one whole share, the warrant costs €10.00. The warrant premium is 10% for half a year, or around 20% a year. The model would have given €7.63 for the same option. The difference is the margin of the issuer, which sets the price itself and uses its own volatility assumption in doing so. More on this follows in the lesson on leveraged products.

bloecke.md: The loss of time value is economically real, but for tax purposes it only counts when the position is sold or expires. Gains from derivative transactions (Termingeschäfte) are covered by Section 20(2) sentence 1 no. 3 EStG (Income Tax Act), and option writer's premiums collected are covered by Section 20(1) no. 11 EStG. Under Section 20(6) EStG, losses remain within capital income and may never be offset against employment income or rental income. The former special limit of €20,000 a year for derivative transactions was abolished without replacement by the Annual Tax Act 2024 (Jahressteuergesetz) of 2 December 2024 and no longer applies in any open cases. The gain is subject to 25% capital income withholding tax (Kapitalertragsteuer) plus solidarity surcharge, 26.375% in total, plus church tax where applicable. The saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag) is €1,000, or €2,000 for joint assessment (Section 20(9) EStG). This information is for orientation only and does not replace tax advice.

The intrinsic value can be calculated directly; the time value is the price of uncertainty. Only the time value inevitably falls to zero, with the square root of the remaining term, that is, late and then fast.

mitnehmen: Every premium is made up of intrinsic value and time value, and options out of the money consist of 100% time value.
The time value is greatest at the money and inevitably falls to zero by expiry, in proportion to the square root of the remaining term and therefore fastest at the end.
Six variables determine the price, namely the price of the underlying, strike price, remaining term, volatility, interest rate and dividend, and only volatility cannot be read off.
Put-call parity, C − P = S − K·e^(−rT), follows solely from arbitrage and needs no valuation model; it also explains why volatility moves the call and the put by the same amount.
The right direction is not enough, because too little movement, too little time or too high a time value at entry can still lead to a total loss.

begriffe.text: The amount that immediate exercise of an option would bring in: max(S − K, 0) for a call, max(K − S, 0) for a put. It can never be negative.
Premium minus intrinsic value, that is, the price paid for the fact that something can still happen before expiry. It is greatest at the money and inevitably falls to zero by the expiry date.
Position of the price relative to the strike price: in the money (with intrinsic value), at the money (price roughly equal to the strike price) or out of the money (without intrinsic value).
Arbitrage relationship for European options with the same strike price and expiry: C − P = S − K·e^(−rT). It holds independently of any valuation model.

Extra cost of acquiring the underlying via a warrant compared with buying it directly, expressed as a percentage of the underlying. For warrants in the money or at the money, the warrant premium corresponds to the time value; for warrants out of the money, the distance between strike price and price is added.
